title: City payees in State politics
question: Do organizations the City pays, or the people who work for them, put money into State campaigns, and does it cluster on San Francisco's own legislators or on one day?
finding: The organizations' own money goes to committees, not candidates. Since 2015 organizations the City pays put $1.1 million of their own money into State political committees; the largest recipient was NPH Action Fund Political Issues Committee ($625,000 from 4 of them); Abode Services gave $325,545; Mercy Housing California gave $320,000; Sequoia Living gave $125,000; Low Income Investment Fund gave $120,000. Their staff gave $379,359 ($210,259 from nonprofit staff, the rest from school, college and university employees), of which $48,466 went to the Assembly and Senate committees of San Francisco's own legislators. Only 3 same-day groups of three or more co-workers appear, the largest 5 people giving $1,450 to Jane Kim for Senate 2016 on 2015-12-27. 5 officer-level gifts of $5,000 or more in a cycle were found. No organization that received a grant from the State Treasurer's or Attorney General's office shows gifts to candidates for that office.
how: Read the 14,689 lines of the Secretary of State's contribution file that name one of the 233 organizations the City paid $5 million or more, either as the giver or as the giver's employer. Kept gifts dated 2015 to 2026 on the latest version of each report (the lines the file labels schedules A and C), one line per giver, committee, date and amount. Left out: 136 lines coded X, which in this file name the same candidate's earlier committee as the go-between and so repeat an earlier gift; and $366,200 recorded by the ActBlue committees, because the same gifts appear again, with ActBlue named as intermediary, at the committee that finally received them. San Francisco's legislators are the names listed in the folder notes for the State files; a statewide office is read from the committee's name. An officer is named only when the same first and last name is on that organization's own tax return as an officer, director or key employee, and the State record shows $5,000 or more in one two-year cycle.
limits: Staff give with their own money. The employer is whatever the giver wrote, so this is a name match: staff who wrote a different name are missed. Only organizations the City paid $5 million or more were searched, and matches on shortened names were dropped as unreliable. A committee under an organization's own name looks like that organization accounting for its own campaign work. A school district shown as giving to a teachers' union committee is most likely forwarding payroll deductions. The State files on disk do not say which statewide office regulates which organization; the only link available is whether that office appears as a grant-maker to it in the State grants file. People who work together often give together after a fundraiser.
